Andrew Jackson (March 15, 1767 - June 8, 1845) was the seventh president of the United States from 1829 to 1837.
Married to Benazir Bhutto in 1987, this politician later served two separate terms as Pakistan's president, decades apart — who is he?
Asif Ali Zardari (born 26 July 1955) is a Pakistani politician who has served as the 14th president of Pakistan since 2024.

Christian IX (8 April 1818 - 29 January 1906) was King of Denmark from 15 November 1863 until his death in 1906.

David Duke (born July 1, 1950) is an American former politician, white supremacist, neo-Nazi, conspiracy theorist, and former grand wizard of the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan.

Edmund Burke (12 January 1729 - 9 July 1797) was an Anglo-Irish writer, philosopher, and politician who is widely credited as the founder of the cultural and political philosophy of conservatism.

Evan Ryan is an American public servant who served as White House cabinet secretary in the administration of Joe Biden.

Félix Faure (30 January 1841 - 16 February 1899) was President of France from 1895 until his death in 1899.

Grand Duchy of Tuscany was an Italian monarchy located in Central Italy that existed, with interruptions, from 1569 to 1860, replacing the Republic of Florence.
A military theorist and champion of the "blitzkrieg," this German general was central to inventing the panzer division and led armoured units in the invasions of Poland and France — who was he?
Heinz Guderian (17 June 1888 - 14 May 1954) was a German army general and military theorist.
This former CEO of security-scanner firm Nuctech has served as Communist Party secretary of Lishui and mayor of Jiaxing — and is the son of a former paramount leader of China. Who is he?

A former Carlyle Group partner and investment banker, this attorney served as the 16th chair of the Federal Reserve from 2018 to 2026 — who is he?
Jerome Powell (born February 4, 1953) is an American central banker and attorney who served as the 16th chair of the Federal Reserve from 2018 to 2026.
Rising from vice president after her predecessor's death, this Malawian educator and activist became her country's first female president in 2012. Who is she?
Joyce Banda (ne Ntila; born 12 April 1950) is a Malawian politician, educator, and activist who served as the fourth president of Malawi from 2012 to 2014.

The youngest Nobel laureate in history, she won the 2014 Peace Prize at 17 for championing girls' education in Pakistan's Swat district — who is she?

This Argentine, a civil engineer by training who founded the centre-right PRO party, governed Buenos Aires before serving as the country's president from 2015 to 2019. Who is he?
Mauricio Macri (born 8 February 1959) is an Argentine businessman and politician who served as President of Argentina from 2015 to 2019.

Born in 1942, this Republican has held the Senate seat from Kentucky since 1985 and was the longest-serving senator in the state's history. He served as Senate Republican leader for 18 years across three stints. Who is he?

Oliver North (born October 7, 1943) is an American political commentator, television host, military historian, author, and retired United States Marine Corps lieutenant colonel.
This historical region in southwestern Iran, corresponding to Fars province, saw Iranic-speaking migrants arrive from Central Asia in ancient times — what is it called?
Persis is a historical region in south-western Iran, roughly corresponding with Fars province.
This Chinese diplomat went from ambassador to the U.S. to foreign minister, then vanished from public view in mid-2023 and was removed from the post that July. Who is he?

This American author built a personal-finance empire around a bestselling book contrasting the money lessons of two father figures, despite later class-action lawsuits and one of his companies filing for bankruptcy — who is he?
Robert Kiyosaki (born April 8, 1947) is an American businessman, entrepreneur, and author, known for the Rich Dad Poor Dad series of personal finance books.

Named after a 1930s guerrilla leader who resisted U.S. occupation, this socialist Nicaraguan political party overthrew dictator Anastasio Somoza Debayle in the 1979 revolution, ending decades of his family's rule — what is it?

In what year did Nikola Tesla die?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
In what year was Chlorine discovered?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
Mikoyan MiG-35: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Marketed as a 4++ generation jet fighter, it is a further development of the MiG-29M/M2 and MiG-29K/KUB fighters.
Which country is HAL Tejas from?
HAL Tejas: India. The aircraft made its first flight in 2001 and entered into service with the IAF in 2015.
Who is credited with discovering Apus?
Apus: Petrus Plancius. Apus is a small constellation in the southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Cat's Eye Nebula?
Cat's Eye Nebula: William Herschel. It is a well-studied object that has been observed from radio to X-ray wavelengths.
Who is credited with discovering Hydrogen?
Hydrogen: Henry Cavendish. Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
Who is credited with discovering Astatine?
Astatine: Emilio G. Segrè. Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
This French surgeon won the 1912 Nobel for pioneering vascular suturing, then teamed up with aviator Charles Lindbergh to build the first perfusion pump for organ transplantation. Who was he?
Alexis Carrel (28 June 1873 - 5 November 1944) was a French surgeon and biologist who spent most of his scientific career in the United States.
Dating back to the Neolithic Revolution around 13,000 BC, this branch of agriculture covers the breeding, feeding, and day-to-day care of livestock raised for meat, milk, or fiber — what's it called?
Animal husbandry is the branch of agriculture concerned with animals that are raised for meat, fibre, milk, or other products.

This German philosopher's 1818 masterwork describes the visible world as the manifestation of a blind, irrational underlying will, building on Kantian idealism while rejecting German idealism's optimism — who is he?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 - 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.

An Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean, it is one of two living members of the family Monodontidae and is also known as the white whale (the only cetacean regularly occurring with this color) and the sea canary for its high-pitched calls. What is it?
Beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean.
This rigid, mineralized organ of the vertebrate skeleton produces both red and white blood cells and helps regulate the body's acid-base balance — what is it?
Bone is a rigid organ that constitutes part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals.
This soft, silvery-white metal shares group 12 of the periodic table with zinc and mercury, resembling zinc in its chemistry and mercury in its low melting point — what element, symbol Cd, is it?
Cadmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cd and atomic number 48.

Derived from the amino acid tyrosine and fifty percent bound to plasma proteins in your bloodstream, what class of neurotransmitter has a benzene ring topped with two hydroxyl groups plus a side-chain amine?

Catecholamine (abbreviated CA), most typically a 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine, is a monoamine neurotransmitter, an organic compound that has a catechol (benzene with two hydroxyl side groups next to each other) and a side-chain amine.
Most species of this loud insect superfamily emerge annually, but a few North American ones famously emerge en masse only once every several years. What insects are they?
Cicada are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).
Known by a colorful nickname, this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye turns it pink, may leave it stuck shut by morning, and spreads easily — what is it?
Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
As of December 2025 worth an estimated $8.7 billion, this Swedish businessman founded and chairs a massive music-streaming company — who is he?
Daniel Ek (Swedish; born 21 February 1983) is a Swedish businessman and technologist.

England-born but raised in Australia, this geologist did much of his real rock-hunting in the Flinders Ranges — though he's better remembered for braving the ice alongside Shackleton on the Nimrod Expedition; who was he?
Douglas Mawson (5 May 1882 - 14 October 1958) was an Australian geologist, Antarctic explorer, and academic.
What medical condition, caused by viruses like herpes simplex or rabies, bacteria, or autoimmune disease, refers to inflammation of the brain and can cause confusion, seizures, and memory problems?

Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain. The severity can be variable with symptoms including reduction or alteration in consciousness, aphasia, headache, fever, confusion, a stiff neck, and vomiting.

Mostly caused by a mutation in the PRNP gene, this neurodegenerative prion disease begins with gradually worsening sleep trouble and progresses to total sleeplessness, speech and coordination problems, and death within months — which disease?
Fatal insomnia is a neurodegenerative prion disease that results in trouble sleeping as its hallmark symptom.

This American mechanical engineer and pioneering management consultant wrote a 1909 book that Academy of Management fellows later voted the most influential management book of the entire 20th century — who was he?
Frederick Winslow Taylor (March 20, 1856 - March 21, 1915) was an American mechanical engineer.
Built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine, this tripeptide is the most abundant low-molecular-mass thiol in most cells and a key antioxidant guarding against free radicals — what is it?
Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide made of the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.

Element 108's isotope 270 carries magic numbers of protons and neutrons that shore it up against fission, yet the most stable forms last only about ten seconds — which synthetic superheavy element is it?
Hassium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Hs and atomic number 108.
Running from the shoulder to the elbow, this arm bone connects the scapula to the radius and ulna, with a rounded head and neck at one end and two epicondyles at the other — name this bone?
Humerus (pl.: humeri) is a long bone in the arm that runs from the shoulder to the elbow.
This Belgian-American physicist-mathematician and 1992 MacArthur Fellow is best known for harnessing wavelets to compress images — a tool so foundational it bears her name. Who is she?
Ingrid Daubechies (doh-bə-SHEE; born 17 August 1954) is a Belgian-American physicist and mathematician at Duke University.
A former Chicago financial options trader, this internet entrepreneur co-founded a nonprofit free encyclopedia as well as the for-profit wiki host Fandom — who is he?
Jimmy Wales (born August 8, 1966) is an American and British internet entrepreneur and former financial trader.
About the size of a domestic chicken, these flightless New Zealand natives turn out to be more closely related to Madagascar's extinct elephant birds than to the giant moa — what are they?
Kiwi (bird) are flightless birds endemic to New Zealand of the order Apterygiformes.
Named for the Latin word for weighing scales and lying between Virgo and Scorpius, this faint zodiac constellation has no first-magnitude stars — which one?
Libra (constellation) is a constellation of the zodiac and is located in the Southern celestial hemisphere.

While at IBM in the 1960s, this computer scientist invented a key technique behind the out-of-order execution most modern processors use — then was fired in 1968 for planning a gender transition, an act IBM apologized for in 2020. Who was this engineer?
Lynn Conway (January 2, 1938 - June 9, 2024) was an American computer scientist, electrical engineer, and transgender rights activist.
A German historian, jurist, and political economist born in 1864, he is counted among the central founders of sociology and still shapes social theory today — who was he?

Max Weber (21 April 1864 - 14 June 1920) was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist who was one of the central figures in the development of sociology and the social sciences more generally.
Widowed in 2021, this Israeli-American billionaire physician publishes Israel Hayom and has been among the most prominent financial supporters of a US president since 2016 — who is she?
Miriam Adelson (ne Farbstein; born October 10, 1945) is an Israeli-American physician, businesswoman, philanthropist, and conservative political donor.
This protective plate at fingertips and toe-tips is found in nearly every primate except marmosets, and is made of the same tough protein found in claws, hooves, and horns — what is it?

Nail (anatomy) is a protective plate characteristically found at the tip of the digits (fingers and toes) of almost all primates (except for marmosets), corresponding to the claws in other tetrapod animals.
Built from proteins, DNA, and RNA around specific chromosomal regions, this nuclear structure is being studied as a target for cancer chemotherapy — what is it?
Nucleolus (pl.: nucleoli) is the largest structure in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.
Founded as a science by Georges Cuvier in 1796, when he demonstrated evidence for extinction, this field studies prehistoric life mainly through fossils — what's the discipline?
Paleontology is the scientific study of the life of the past, mainly but not exclusively through the study of fossils.
Which management theorist and educator's writings on organizing business, government, and nonprofit sectors made him one of the most influential thinkers on modern management?

Peter Drucker (November 19, 1909 - November 11, 2005) was an Austrian American management consultant, educator, and author, whose writings contributed to the philosophical and practical foundations of modern management theory.
This genus of single-celled parasites moves from mosquito to human bloodstream, destroying red blood cells and causing a disease with recurring fevers — what is this genus called?
Plasmodium is a genus of unicellular eukaryotes that are obligate parasites of vertebrates and insects.

Derived enzymatically from a fatty acid found in nearly every tissue of the body, this class of lipid compounds produces diverse hormone-like effects despite not being true hormones — what are they called?
Prostaglandin (PG) are a group of physiologically active lipid compounds that have diverse hormone-like effects in animals.
Along with his two brothers, this American physician-turned-businessman acquired the pharmaceutical company behind OxyContin, later linked to the U.S. opioid crisis — who is he?
Raymond Sackler (February 16, 1920 - July 17, 2017) was an American physician and businessman.

Named after the naturalist who first documented it, this highly venomous South Asian snake is known for an extremely painful bite and ranks among the region's 'Big Four' dangerous species — what snake is it?
Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) is a species of highly venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
This interdisciplinary field studies signs and sign systems, breaking down into branches examining the formal relations between signs, their meanings, and their users — what's the field called?
Semiotics is the study of signs. It is an interdisciplinary field that examines what signs are, how they form sign systems, and how individuals use them to communicate meaning.
This plant family includes both deadly poisonous species and kitchen staples like tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers, all linked by unusually high alkaloid content — what family is it?
Solanaceae is a family of flowering plants in the order Solanales.
This colorless, sweet-smelling liquid with the formula C6H5CH=CH2 is manufactured from benzene as the industrial precursor to a widely used plastic — what compound is it?
Styrene is an organic compound with the chemical formula C6H5CH=CH2.
A colorless, water-miscible cyclic ether and a versatile solvent, this compound is mainly used as a precursor to polymers and is an isomer of butanone — what is it?
Tetrahydrofuran (THF), or oxolane, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2)4O.
When water loss to the air outpaces uptake by the roots, plants shut tiny leaf pores to conserve moisture, slowing this evaporative water-movement process — what's it called?
Transpiration is the process of water movement through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts, such as leaves, stems and flowers.
Native only to the wetlands of the Carolinas, which carnivorous plant snaps shut a 'jaw' formed from the tips of its leaves when an insect trips it?
Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is a carnivorous plant native to the temperate and subtropical wetlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States.
This noble gas, found in trace amounts in Earth's atmosphere, powers arc lamps, serves as a rare anesthetic, and was the first of its family coaxed into a genuine chemical compound — which element?
Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Named for the skull-shaped marking on its thorax and first classified by Carl Linnaeus in 1758, this large moth was immortalized on the poster for 'The Silence of the Lambs' — which insect?
Acherontia atropos: Species of moth. It is most commonly identified by the vaguely skull-shaped pattern adorning the thorax, the characteristic from which its common and scientific names are derived.
Scientifically named Gadus chalcogrammus, this schooling member of the cod family gathers in massive numbers in the eastern Bering Sea — which fish?
Alaska pollock: Species of fish. The Alaska pollock also known as Pacific pollock or walleye pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus) is a marine fish species of the cod genus Gadus and family Gadidae.
Nicknamed 'whip-spiders' or 'tailless whip-scorpions,' these arachnids have no silk, no venom, and a name meaning 'blunt tail' — they grab with their pedipalps instead of biting — what order is this?
Amblypygi: Order of arachnids. The name "amblypygid" means "blunt tail", a reference to a lack of the flagellum that is otherwise seen in whip-scorpions.
Brought to Asia by Spanish traders aboard the Manila galleons, this tropical American tree produces a knobby, sweet fruit known as sugar apple or custard apple — what is this plant?
Annona squamosa: Species of tree. Annona squamosa is a small, well-branched tree or shrub from the family Annonaceae that bears edible fruits called sugar apples or sweetsops or custard apples.

Known only from fragmentary remains including vertebrae and a giant femur first found by a farmer in 1987, this titanosaur may be the largest land animal ever discovered, stretching up to 35 meters — which genus?
Argentinosaurus: Late Cretaceous giant sauropod dinosaur genus.
This category of illness occurs when the body's adaptive immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissue, with more than 80 recognized forms identified so far — what's the category?
Autoimmune disease: Disorders of adaptive immune system. Autoimmune diseases are a separate class from autoinflammatory diseases.
Sharing its engine, transmission, and rotor system with the Huey utility helicopter, this rapidly-developed attack chopper became America's dedicated gunship escort in the Vietnam War — what is it?
Bell AH-1 Cobra: Family of attack helicopters.
This organ stores urine received from the kidneys via the ureters before it exits through the urethra, and gives us the medical term 'cystitis' when inflamed — what is it?
Bladder: Organ in vertebrates that collects and stores urine from the kidneys before disposal.
Named from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart,' this condition means a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes normal in well-conditioned athletes — which condition?
Bradycardia: Heart rate below the normal range.
Native to the Americas from Patagonia to western Canada, members of this succulent plant family thrive in the bone-dry Atacama Desert — what are they?
Cactus: Family of mostly succulent plants, adapted to dry environments.

A German child prodigy turned director of the Göttingen Observatory, this mathematician, astronomer, and physicist made landmark contributions across number theory, algebra, statistics, and probability — who is he?
Carl Friedrich Gauss: German polymath and scholar (1777–1855)
This Italian physician who died in 1909 is considered the founder of modern criminology, arguing that 'born criminals' could be spotted by physical defects — who is he?
Add this steely-grey transition metal (atomic number 24) to steel and you get stainless; polish it and it reflects nearly 70% of visible light without tarnishing. Which element is it?
Chromium: Chemical element with atomic number 24 (Cr)
Also known as ubiquinone, this antioxidant cofactor helps mitochondria produce ATP and gets its name from ten isoprenyl units in its molecular tail — what is it?
Coenzyme Q10: Biochemical cofactor and antioxidant. Coenzyme Q (CoQ), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring biochemical cofactor (coenzyme) and an antioxidant produced by the human body.
This group of RNA viruses, named for the club-shaped spikes that crown their surface, causes illnesses ranging from the common cold to SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what are they called?
Coronavirus: Subfamily of viruses in the family Coronaviridae.
Named after the bladder because it was first found in urine, this amino acid carries a thiol group that lets it forge the disulfide bonds holding many proteins together. Which amino acid is it?
Cysteine: Proteinogenic amino acid. Cysteine (symbol Cys or C) is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid with the formula HS−CH2−CH(NH2)−COOH.
Native to South and Southeast Asia, this is the sole species in its genus and lives in large, non-hierarchical clans with several breeding females — what's this wild canid called?
Dhole: Species of mammal. The dhole ( dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia.

With nearly 24,000 ommatidia in each compound eye and wings usually held flat rather than folded, this iridescent flying insect is often confused with its lighter-bodied damselfly cousins — what is it?
The largest living land animal comes in three recognized species and counts mammoths and mastodons among its extinct cousins — what is it?
Elephant: Largest living land animal. The trunk is prehensile, bringing food and water to the mouth and grasping objects.
Marketed as Lexapro, this SSRI treats depression and anxiety but is exclusively sold commercially as an oxalate salt — what is it?

Escitalopram: SSRI antidepressant. It is mainly used to treat major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), and social anxiety disorder.
With a black-tipped bushy tail and brownish-grey striped fur, this small wild feline lives in Scotland, Turkey, the Caucasus, and mainland forests, hunting rodents and ground birds — which species?
European wildcat: Small wild cat. The European wildcat (Felis silvestris) is a small wildcat species that was described in the late 18th century.
This beetle family produces light mainly at twilight to attract mates — though some females mimic another species' flash pattern just to lure and eat the males — what are they commonly called?
Firefly: Family of beetles. The Lampyridae are a family of elateroid beetles with more than 2,400 described species, many of which are light-emitting.
Traditionally pounded from cassava, plantains, and cocoyam, this West African staple gets a shoutout in Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart — what dish is it?
Fufu: Dough-like food in African cuisine.
The largest of its family, this mostly solitary mammal uses long foreclaws to dig into nests and a sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites — what animal is it?
Giant anteater: Species of mammal. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
Dating back roughly 250 million years to the early Triassic, this ground-dwelling insect hears through an organ on its abdomen and leaps away from danger using powerful hind legs — what is it?
Grasshopper: Common name for a group of insects.

This Austrian physician who coined "autistic psychopathy" lent his name to a syndrome, but later faced allegations he referred disabled children to a Vienna clinic that killed hundreds during the Nazi era — who was he?
Found in trace amounts in modern gasoline blends, this colorless, six-carbon alkane boils at about 69°C and serves as a cheap, low-reactivity solvent — what is it?
A colorless gas that throws off white fumes the moment it meets moist air, it turns into a familiar strong acid once dissolved in water — which compound, formula HCl?
Hydrogen chloride: Chemical compound. Hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid are important in technology and industry.

Also known as the spectacled or binocellate snake, this reptile from South Asia is one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebites in the region and is revered in Hindu mythology — which snake?
Indian cobra: Species of snake. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent, and is a member of the "Big Four" species that are responsible for the most snakebite cases in Sri Lanka and India.
This English inventor and industrial designer created the bagless vacuum cleaner using cyclonic separation, and by 2023 was the UK's fifth-richest person — who is he?
James Dyson: British inventor and businessman (born 1947)
Back in 1859, this Irish physicist proved the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect — who was he?
Deafened by childhood illness and rerouted from competitive diving, she became a Hollywood stunt pioneer and earned the title 'the fastest woman in the world.' Who was she?
Kitty O'Neil: American stuntwoman and racer (1946–2018)
This small Arctic rodent is the unwitting star of a persistent myth that it hurls itself off cliffs in mass suicide — what is it?
Lemming: Tribe of rodents of the family Cricetidae.

A domesticated South American camelid whose Quechua name the Spanish adopted, this herd animal can haul about a quarter of its body weight for miles and learns simple tasks after a few tries — what is it?
Llama: Species of wooly domesticated mammal.
Popular as companion birds despite conservation concerns for several species, these large, long-tailed, brightly colored New World parrots belong to the tribe Arini — what are they?
Macaw: Group of birds in the parrot family.
On April 3, 1973, this Motorola engineer made history's first public call from a handheld cell phone on a Manhattan sidewalk — who is he?
Cataloged as a nebula by a French astronomer in 1781, this supergiant elliptical galaxy boasts roughly 15,000 globular clusters, a hundred times more than our own — which galaxy is it?
Messier 87: Galaxy in the constellation Virgo.
Developed in Germany in the late 1800s from the smallest members of a larger breed to create an efficient ratter, this pint-sized dog remains one of the most popular breeds worldwide — which breed?
Miniature Schnauzer: German breed of dog. Miniature Schnauzers are recognized in four colors internationally: solid black, black and silver, salt and pepper, and white.
In this autoimmune disease the immune system attacks myelin, the insulation around nerve cells, so the central nervous system can't transmit signals properly — what condition?
Multiple sclerosis: Disease that damages the myelin sheaths around nerves.
Commonly called horsehair worms, these parasitoid animals get their nickname from the Gordian knot because of how they tangle themselves up — what phylum is this?

Nematomorpha: Phylum of parasitoid animals; horsehair worms. The adult worms are free-living, but the larvae are parasitic on arthropods, such as beetles, cockroaches, mantises, orthopterans, and crustaceans.

A French apothecary and physician who studied at Avignon until the plague closed it, he's far better remembered for 942 cryptic quatrains said to foretell the future — by what Latinised name is he known?
Nostradamus: French apothecary, astrologer and seer (1503–1566)
Sold under the brand name Tamiflu, this oral antiviral is recommended for high-risk patients within 48 hours of their first flu symptoms. What drug is it?
Oseltamivir: Antiviral medication used against influenza.
Believed to have originated in Sardinia and first cultivated in Britain in 1548, which herb is often used simply as a garnish today?
Parsley: Species of flowering plant in the celery family Apiaceae cultivated as an herb.
Dubbed 'the champion of management as a serious discipline,' this Austrian-American writer popularized the concept of management by objectives — who is he?
Peter Drucker: American management consultant and author (1909–2005)

Cultivated for its edible nuts since prehistoric times and native to the Mediterranean and the Levant, this pine species has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — which species?
Pinus pinea: Species of pine tree. Pinus pinea, the Italian stone pine or Mediterranean stone pine, is a tree from the pine family, Pinaceae.
Stockpiled for radiation emergencies, this oral compound floods and shields the thyroid gland — and also treats hyperthyroidism and the skin infection sporotrichosis. Which compound is it?
Fossils of this genus, found in Germany's Solnhofen limestone, mark the first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile — which genus?
Pterodactylus: Genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic.
Belonging to the genus Corvus and distinguished from its close relatives mainly by size, the largest species in this bird category are also the largest of all perching birds — which bird?
Raven: Index of animals with the same common name.
This Israeli-American mathematician shared the 2005 Nobel in Economics with Thomas Schelling for illuminating conflict and cooperation through game theory — who is he?
Caused by bacteria in the Salmonella genus, this common form of food poisoning brings diarrhea, fever, and cramps within 12 to 36 hours of eating contaminated food — what is it called?
Salmonellosis: Infection caused by Salmonella bacteria. It is one of the most common diseases to be known as food poisoning (though the name refers to food-borne illness in general).
People with this anxiety disorder are fully capable of speech but fall silent in specific situations or around specific people, even when staying quiet brings shame or punishment — what is it called?
Selective mutism: Anxiety disorder blocking speech. Selective mutism usually co-exists with social anxiety disorder.
This layer of tissue covering a vertebrate's body serves three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation?
Skin: Soft outer covering organ of vertebrates.

Once meaning a Christian life oriented toward the Holy Spirit, this concept broadened over centuries to describe a subjective sense of the sacred and 'the deepest values and meanings by which people live,' often apart from organized religion. What's the term?
NATO nicknamed this Soviet variable-sweep-wing tactical bomber 'Fencer'; it was the USSR's first plane with an integrated digital navigation-and-attack system — which aircraft is it?
Sukhoi Su-24: Family of Soviet strike aircraft.
Once the thylacine went extinct in 1936, this stocky, screeching marsupial — now confined to a single island — became the world's largest carnivorous marsupial; what is it?
Tasmanian devil: Australian carnivorous marsupial. The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii; palawa kani: purinina) is a carnivorous marsupial of the family Dasyuridae.
With a half-life of roughly 14 billion years — about the age of the universe — the most stable isotope of this weakly radioactive metal decays into stable lead-208. Which element is it?
Thorium: Chemical element with atomic number 90 (Th)
Usually caused by a new genetic mutation rather than inherited, which disorder produces deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones, and chin but typically leaves intelligence normal?
Treacher Collins syndrome: Human genetic disorder. The degree to which a person is affected may vary from mild to severe.
A breakdown product of purine nucleotides found naturally in urine, elevated blood levels of this heterocyclic compound can trigger gout and kidney stones — what is it?
Uric acid: Organic compound. Uric acid is a heterocyclic compound of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen with the formula C5H4N4O3.
Many of these 23 carrion-eating birds sport a bald head to stay clean while feeding, and cool off by urinating on their own legs — what kind of bird is it?
Vulture: Common name for a type of bird.

A physician by training, this Polish politician has served as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence since 2023, after leading his country's labour ministry a decade earlier — who is he?
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz: Polish physician and politician (born 1981)
What is the chemical symbol for neptunium?
The symbol for neptunium is Np. Neptunium is a chemical element; it has symbol Np and atomic number 93.
Europium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for europium is Eu. Europium is a chemical element; it has symbol Eu and atomic number 63.

In what year was Song Hye-kyo born?
Song Hye-kyo (Korean: 송혜교; born November 22, 1981) is a South Korean actress.
In what year was Julie Andrews born?
Julie Andrews: Dame Julie Andrews (born Julia Elizabeth Wells, 1 October 1935) is an English actress, singer and author.
In what year was Kristen Bell born?
Kristen Bell: Kristen Anne Bell (born July 18, 1980) is an American actress and singer.
In what year was Kelsey Grammer born?
Kelsey Grammer: Allen Kelsey Grammer (born February 21, 1955) is an American actor.
In what year was Jada Pinkett Smith born?
Jada Pinkett Smith: Jada Koren Pinkett Smith (née Pinkett; born September 18, 1971) is an American actress, businesswoman, talk show host and singer.
In what year was Kerry Von Erich born?
Kerry Von Erich: Kerry Gene Adkisson (February 3, 1960 – February 18, 1993), better known by his ring name Kerry Von Erich, was an American professional wrestler.
In what year was Elvis Presley born?
Elvis Presley: Elvis Aaron Presley (January 8, 1935 – August 16, 1977) was an American singer and actor.

Caitlyn Jenner: Caitlyn Marie Jenner (born William Bruce Jenner, October 28, 1949), is an American media personality and retired Olympic gold medal-winning decathlete.

Sean Penn: Sean Justin Penn (born August 17, 1960) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Kenneth Branagh born?
Kenneth Branagh: Sir Kenneth Charles Branagh ( BRAN-ə; born 10 December 1960) is a British actor and filmmaker.

Dylan Sprouse: Dylan Thomas Sprouse (born August 4, 1992) is an American actor.
In what year did Burt Reynolds die?
Burt Reynolds: Burton Leon Reynolds Jr. (February 11, 1936 – September 6, 2018) was an American actor.
In what year did Cary Grant die?
Cary Grant (born Archibald Alec Leach; 18 January 1904 – 29 November 1986) was an English-American actor.
In what year was Die Hard with a Vengeance first released?
Die Hard with a Vengeance: It is the sequel to Die Hard (1988) and Die Hard 2 (1990) and the third installment in the Die Hard film series.
